A maximum-severity security flaw impacting the Bricksforge plugin for WordPress has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to Patchstack.

The critical vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-85097 (CVSS score: 10.0), which allows unauthenticated attackers to upload and execute arbitrary PHP code on vulnerable WordPress websites, resulting in remote code execution (RCE). The security flaw impacts Bricksforge versions up to and including 3.1.8.9. Patches have been released in version 3.1.8.10.

Bricksforge is a WordPress plugin that's advertised as a "Swiss Army knife" for Bricks, a visual website-building tool for WordPress, with support for animations, advanced forms, and scrolling video sequences.

WordPress security company Patchstack said it detected exploitation efforts targeting the flaw on October 7, 2026, at 9:47 p.m. UTC.

"Bricksforge validates a file's MIME type when it is first uploaded. When a form is later submitted, however, it trusts the file metadata the client sends," Patchstack said. "In particular, it does not validate the 'url' field inside the 'temporaryFileUploads' parameter."

At a high level, the vulnerability stems from insufficient validation of a URL field in the 'temporaryFileUploads' parameter during form submission. An attacker could exploit this loophole to achieve RCE through four steps -

  • Request a valid nonce from the unauthenticated 'bricksforge_regenerate_nonce' AJAX endpoint.
  • Upload a GIF/PHP polyglot: a file that is a valid image but also contains PHP code. It passes the MIME check and lands in the temporary upload directory.
  • Submit a form where the 'file' path points to that validated image, but the 'url' ends in a PHP extension.
  • Bricksforge implicitly trusts the submitted metadata and places the file's contents at the PHP location, leading to the execution of the embedded code when that file is requested.

"An unauthenticated attacker can first obtain a valid nonce via the bricksforge_regenerate_nonce AJAX endpoint, then upload a GIF/PHP polyglot file to the temporary upload directory where MIME type validation is correctly performed," Wordfence said in an advisory for the flaw.

"Subsequently, the attacker can submit a form with a crafted 'temporaryFileUploads' parameter where the server-side file path points to the validated GIF file, but the attacker-controlled url field ends with a .php extension."

Successful exploitation of the flaw could result in arbitrary PHP execution on the server, which an attacker can leverage to seize control of the WordPress site, deploy web shells, read sensitive data, and establish persistent access. 

In the attacks observed by Patchstack, threat actors have been observed targeting the Bricksforge REST API form submission endpoint ("/wp-json/bricksforge/v1/form_submit") or the "/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php" endpoint with "bricksforge_form_submit" action along with a crafted "temporaryFileUploads" parameter.

A representative request is as follows -

{
  "temporaryFileUploads": [
    {
      "field": "form-field-file",
      "file": {
        "file": "/var/www/example.com/wp-content/uploads/bricksforge/tmp/img_example.gif",
        "url": "https://example.com/wp-content/uploads/bricksforge/tmp/img_example.php",
        "type": "image/gif"
      }
    }
  ]
}

As highlighted by Wordfence, threat actors are exploiting a mismatch where the specified "file" argument is a GIF (or a PNG) file, while the actual URL points to a PHP payload.

To get around extension filtering, the exploitation activity makes use of alternate PHP extensions (e.g., .php5, .php7, or .phtml), case manipulation (e.g., .PHP, .Php, or .pHp), and encoded extensions (e.g., .%70hp, %2ephp, or .%2570%2568%2570).

"Two clusters stand out in our telemetry. In the first, 44 IPs sent 56 requests with identical payloads within seconds of each other," Patchstack said. "In the second, three IPs tested 25 variations of PHP extensions and encodings against the same temporary file."

"Both patterns point to automated exploitation over rotating proxies or distributed infrastructure. They do not, on their own, attribute the activity to a single threat actor."

  • 23.97.62[.]146
  • 84.247.60[.]125
  • 38.154.185[.]97
  • 150.109.16[.]166
  • 153.75.90[.]146

item.title: Critical SonicWall SMA 1000 Flaw Targeted in 135 Exploitation Attempts After Patch (2026)
item.description:
Threat actors have been observed exploiting a recently disclosed critical security flaw in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) 1000 appliances within days of public disclosure.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score: 10.0), is a case of pre-authenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) that could allow a remote attacker "to direct the appliance to issue requests on their behalf and reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations."

Patches for the flaw were released by SonicWall on October 6, 2026, with versions 12.4.3-03670 (platform-hotfix) and 12.5.0-03082 (platform-hotfix).

The vulnerability has since started witnessing active exploitation attempts, with first signs detected by threat intelligence firms Defused Cyber and Previdian on October 8, 2026.

Data from Previdian shows that a total of 135 attempts have been observed to date from two unique IP addresses located in the U.S. SonicWall has yet to update the advisory to reflect active exploitation of the flaw.

CVE-2026-102255 is the latest vulnerability impacting SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances to come under active exploitation. In June 2026, two other flaws in the same product (CVE-2026-15409, CVSS score: 10.0, and CVE-2026-15410, CVSS score: 7.2) were weaponized as zero-days by a threat actor dubbed UTA0533 to deploy Java web shells and a malware called KNUCKLEBALL.

Rapid7 also said it observed threat actors leveraging the flaws to target internet-facing devices and use them as a stealthy initial access vector to execute commands on the operating system and ensure long-term, persistent access.

"Once they established a foothold on the appliance, the actors systematically extracted high-value credentials, active session databases, and Time-Based One-Time Password (TOTP) multi-factor authentication (MFA) seed configurations," the company noted.

"With these harvested resources, the threat actors quickly shifted to lateral movement, pivoting from the compromised appliance directly into the internal corporate network."

item.title: Ledger Finds Unauthorized Hardware Implant in CryptoBilis-Sold Wallet Amid Fund Theft Reports (2026)
item.description:
Cryptocurrency hardware maker Ledger has temporarily paused sales of its products via CryptoBilis following reports of stolen funds linked to devices sold by the reseller.

On Friday, the company said it was investigating reports of loss of funds from users in Southeast Asia who had purchased products from CryptoBilis. The incident is said to have resulted in losses totaling more than $86 million, according to pseudonymous blockchain investigator Specter.

"We recommend Ledger users who purchased from this reseller in the last 90 days to not initiate set up if you have not done so yet," Ledger said in an X post. "If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with new seed)."

The company has since revealed that one of the impacted users' devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant, and that it's reaching out to impacted users as part of an ongoing probe into the incident. Out of an abundance of caution, CryptoBilis has ceased sales of all hardware wallet inventory until the investigation is concluded.

"Your recovery phrase must be generated by your device when you set it up, and written down by you," CryptoBilis said in an alert on its website. "If your device came with a recovery phrase already printed or written on a card or sheet, or if anyone other than you has seen your recovery phrase, treat your wallet as unsafe."

"Never share your recovery phrase or PIN with anyone. No one from CryptoBilis or Ledger will ever ask for them. Be careful of anyone who offers to recover lost funds; these offers are almost always scams."

In a follow-up update posted on October 11, 2026, Ledger acknowledged that the CryptoBilis incident has impacted a "limited" number of devices, adding all confirmed cases involve devices sold through CryptoBilis.

The company also advised resellers and distributors to source products only through authorized channels and never to restock returned products.

"Also, we strongly advise users not to purchase from unauthorized resellers, where the risk of buying suspicious, counterfeit or modified devices is important as nothing operates under ledger security guidelines," it added.

Update

In an update shared on October 13, 2026, Ledger said it has not confirmed the total number of affected users or the total value lost following the incidents. It also described the hardware implant as designed to capture a victim's hardware wallet's seed phrase and use it to drain the assets -

The implant sits inside the enclosure and reads the data shown on the screen. During setup, the signer displays the 24-word recovery phrase. When the implant detects these screens, its microcontroller decodes the words and transmits them over LTE using a provisioned eSIM. The implant is a separate component. It does not modify the Secure Element or the Ledger operating system, and it does not alter transactions or signatures.

The findings corroborate a report from Tibane Labs, which detailed three different variants of the implant, each more advanced than its predecessor. The third generation is assessed to be the most sophisticated. It was purchased on Amazon Japan from a third-party seller based in China.

"The parcel was shipped from Malaysia," Tibane Labs said. "The route is worth noting: a listing on a mainstream marketplace, a seller in one country, a shipment from another, and nothing on the box to tell it apart from a genuine new device."

The Paris-based company has since disclosed that MediaMarkt Saturn has paused the sale of Ledger devices in their stores following the discovery of an implant from one customer in Germany. "No loss of funds were reported," it added.

As of writing, Ledger's website shows that sales of its devices have been temporarily paused through the following authorized resellers, although it's unclear if it's related to the same incident -

  • CryptoBilis (Indonesia and Malaysia)
  • Shopee Mall (Malaysia and the Philippines)
  • LazMall (the Philippines)

Ledger has also shared a "Genuine Check" mechanism to determine the hardware integrity of the device. However, it has cautioned users to first take a backup of the recovery phrase, because opening a signer can damage it. It has also explicitly warned that "it cannot detect unauthorized physical modifications to the hardware" if the Secure Element remains intact.

"We have no indication that Ledger's infrastructure, systems or services were compromised," Ledger noted. "Ledger will never call you, message you directly, or ask for your 24-word recovery phrase."

Ledger Expands Pause of Third-Party Sales

Ledger, in an update shared on October 13, 2026, at 6:03 p.m. ET, confirmed it's asking resellers and distributors across Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to suspend the sale of Ledger devices and take them off the shelves as the investigation remains ongoing. Targeted countries include Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Hong Kong.

"To be clear, as the investigation continues, the only confirmed incidents remain contained to Southeast Asia," it said. "We have not verified a drain linked to a device bought elsewhere. The investigation is ongoing to determine who tampered with these devices and where in the distribution chain it happened."

(The story was updated after publication to reflect the latest developments.)

item.title: Bring Your Own Agent: Your Employees' Assistants Are Already Logged In (2026)
item.description:
The personal AI agents rollout is going about as smoothly as expected: Amazon now blocks Meta's Muse because it doesn't identify itself as a bot while browsing; Instinct keeps raising privacy concerns; and the horror stories from pretty much every personal AI agent keep piling up.

Regardless, the tech world is mesmerized by the capabilities and potential of these services. Less than a year after the first release of the open-source agent now called OpenClaw, the juggernauts are putting their weight behind the idea that each of us needs a personal assistant.

You know what's coming: your employees will connect their personal agents to work systems. There's no stopping that. Their agents already manage their home time, and managing their work time is the next logical step. For them, that is. Not for your security.

Given that personal agents will reach corporate systems whether approved or not, you might be wondering what the best way is to block them. If that’s your thinking, we’re here to offer you another path: enable safe usage instead, with identity as the control plane, and reap the benefits.

BYOD, meet BYOA(I)

The Bring-Your-Own-Device shift is the obvious comparison, but calling this the new era of BYOD would undersell the challenges personal AI agents introduce. These aren't just devices presumed to be insecure that contain company data, but entire AIs that act on company systems in the employee’s name.

Bring-Your-Own-AI (or Bring-Your-Own-Agent) is, then, an identity challenge first and foremost. The best-case scenario is an agent wielding identities with an owner of record, limited approval, and no offboarding. You will also have agents who pretend to be employees, and agents with identities that have no easily recognizable owner.

But the main difference between the two movements is where the control point sits. BYOD gave IT a device to enroll. A personal agent is something you can't register: it lives on the vendor's computer or blends into the employee's. And it's likely in your systems today, whether you can see it or not.

How personal agents get in

Whoever connects a personal AI agent to your systems today likely does this without ever filing a ticket. Instead, they connect it the way they'd connect other apps:

  • OAuth consent. The agent requests access to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or Slack, and the employee clicks Allow. If your tenant lets users consent to third-party apps, that's the whole process.
  • A text thread. Take Instinct, for example. Users text it, link their Google, Apple, or Facebook account, and it acts through the services they connect.
  • Saved passwords in the agent's browser. Many of the agents can sign in to supported sites using passwords via a browser and an internal password manager. To your app, it looks like the employee is logging in.
  • API keys and personal access tokens. For unofficial integrations, many agents can use API keys and personal access tokens, which require users to create long-term credentials.
  • The employee's own laptop. A local agent like OpenClaw reaches whatever the machine it's installed on can see. Muse got a Mac app on September 18 that reads files, notes, calendars, and email with the user's permission, and can take optional Full Disk Access. Dots can work from the user's laptop once it's connected. The same goes for AI browsers like Atlassian's Dia, which read your open pages and connect to Slack and Gmail.

Meet the agents

Less than a year into the category, we’re already starting to see sub-categories emerge in the nascent personal AI agent market. Some agents are more corporate, and others are more personal. But you’ll be hard-pressed to find one that’s truly tailored to a work environment in terms of what it does, and, more importantly, doesn’t do.

Take OpenAI’s Dots, for example. It’s as corporate as a product such as this can be. “Specialist dots” will have their own identities and credentials. OpenAI is working with Microsoft to deploy them under Agent 365, and the connectors are based on those created for ChatGPT. Even the rollout is limited to enterprise accounts and high-tier subscriptions. 

xAI’s GrokBot has an R&D distribution channel via Cursor. If your devs have Cursor, they might have access to GrokBot. Here, the idea is to turn the AI bot tied to the work-controlled development environment into a personal assistant, but that doesn’t make it more governed. Like its competitors, GrokBot is more than willing to sign in to tools without using a clean API via its virtual computer. 

Meta’s muse is consumer-first, and currently US and Canada-only. That said, a few weeks after launch, it gained many organizational connectors, including Slack, Linear, and Vercel. It’s also, ostensibly, the fastest-growing personal AI agent in the fall of 2026. 

The buzziest personal AI agent in tech circles is Instinct. It’s a personal AI agent from a small start-up that works through text apps. It can connect to pretty much any work environment. And it has a privacy policy that raised many an eyebrow. Speaking of raising, Instinct itself raised $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation, so it’s one of the best-funded underdogs ever. 

Finally, we’d be remiss if we didn’t mention OpenClaw. The open-source agent that runs on the user’s own machine is adapting to a future where it’s not the only personal AI in town. It’s trying to go “multiplayer,” with several trusted users operating the same bot while adding features like session ownership. 

Everyone is building governance. For their own deployments.

Most of the aforementioned vendors are currently adding controls for managed deployments. So if you trust your employees to use corporate Dots, Grokbot, or Muse, there’s good news aplenty in recent announcements. 

But all of these only work inside a corporate deployment. None of the truly personal AI agents will show up in the relevant admin console. This is not to say that you should necessarily block “unauthorized” agents en masse. Your employees are learning to rely on them, and there’s great productivity improvement potential. 

Instead, treat the agent as an external entity. Someone else runs it, and the employee owns it. What you do have is the other end: the accounts, grants, and sessions it uses inside your systems.

For users, it’s good to have the agents run on a computer in the vendor’s cloud or on their own server. For you, it’s a headache, even if the vendor's architecture is thoughtful. Take Muse, which runs a dedicated VM with a guard called Sentinel that checks every outbound request, and tokens that the agent itself never handles. In other words, the Sentinel enforces the users’ policy rather than the employer's, and corporate session tokens end up on someone else’s computer. 

Local agents running on laptops have the opposite problem. Credentials stay local, but nothing tells the agent apart from the employee.

Enable the agent, govern the identity

So what’s the ideal solution? It looks something like this: employees can benefit from using their personal agent at work, but the workplace controls the reach via identities. 

It means: 

  • Discovering the agents already connected. This is your Shadow AI inventory, which you assemble based on the different ways AI agents access your systems. These can be OAuth grants to agent vendors, sign-ins from vendor cloud ranges, long-lived API keys issued to unknown clients, or EDR findings. 
  • Attributing each agent to a human owner.
  • Right-sizing the agent’s access. A personal agent inherits everything its owner can do, and it's usually asked to do a sliver of that. 
  • Retiring the agent when the owner leaves, including grants, tokens, and sessions that outlive the account.

Easier said than done, obviously, but some of the fundamentals are there. More will likely be added in the coming months to create the connective tissue between personal AI agents and workplaces. For example, we still need to know if whoever signs in with a username and password is an employee or their agent. Agent-to-agent communication isn’t solved yet. And the ability to compartmentalize knowledge, so that a personal agent loses it during offboarding, isn’t here yet.

Additional controls are coming, but you don’t have to wait for the vendors to catch up. Token Security already finds the personal agents connected to your systems, ties each one to its owner, trims its access, and shuts it off when the employee leaves. Identity is the control plane for AI agents and personal agents are no different. See it on your own environment.

How personal agents get in

Whoever connects a personal AI agent to your systems today likely does this without ever filing a ticket. Instead, they connect it the way they'd connect other apps:

  • OAuth consent. The agent requests access to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or Slack, and the employee clicks Allow. If your tenant lets users consent to third-party apps, that's the whole process.
  • A text thread. Take Instinct, for example. Users text it, link their Google, Apple, or Facebook account, and it acts through the services they connect.
  • Saved passwords in the agent's browser. Many of the agents can sign in to supported sites using passwords via a browser and an internal password manager. To your app, it looks like the employee is logging in.
  • API keys and personal access tokens. For unofficial integrations, many agents can use API keys and personal access tokens, which require users to create long-term credentials.
  • The employee's own laptop. A local agent like OpenClaw reaches whatever the machine it's installed on can see. Muse got a Mac app on September 18 that reads files, notes, calendars, and email with the user's permission, and can take optional Full Disk Access. Dots can work from the user's laptop once it's connected. The same goes for AI browsers like Atlassian's Dia, which read your open pages and connect to Slack and Gmail.

Meet the agents

Less than a year into the category, we’re already starting to see sub-categories emerge in the nascent personal AI agent market. Some agents are more corporate, and others are more personal. But you’ll be hard-pressed to find one that’s truly tailored to a work environment in terms of what it does, and, more importantly, doesn’t do.

Take OpenAI’s Dots, for example. It’s as corporate as a product such as this can be. “Specialist dots” will have their own identities and credentials. OpenAI is working with Microsoft to deploy them under Agent 365, and the connectors are based on those created for ChatGPT. Even the rollout is limited to enterprise accounts and high-tier subscriptions. 

xAI’s GrokBot has an R&D distribution channel via Cursor. If your devs have Cursor, they might have access to GrokBot. Here, the idea is to turn the AI bot tied to the work-controlled development environment into a personal assistant, but that doesn’t make it more governed. Like its competitors, GrokBot is more than willing to sign in to tools without using a clean API via its virtual computer. 

Meta’s muse is consumer-first, and currently US and Canada-only. That said, a few weeks after launch, it gained many organizational connectors, including Slack, Linear, and Vercel. It’s also, ostensibly, the fastest-growing personal AI agent in the fall of 2026. 

The buzziest personal AI agent in tech circles is Instinct. It’s a personal AI agent from a small start-up that works through text apps. It can connect to pretty much any work environment. And it has a privacy policy that raised many an eyebrow. Speaking of raising, Instinct itself raised $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation, so it’s one of the best-funded underdogs ever. 

Finally, we’d be remiss if we didn’t mention OpenClaw. The open-source agent that runs on the user’s own machine is adapting to a future where it’s not the only personal AI in town. It’s trying to go “multiplayer,” with several trusted users operating the same bot while adding features like session ownership. 

Everyone is building governance. For their own deployments.

Most of the aforementioned vendors are currently adding controls for managed deployments. So if you trust your employees to use corporate Dots, Grokbot, or Muse, there’s good news aplenty in recent announcements. 

But all of these only work inside a corporate deployment. None of the truly personal AI agents will show up in the relevant admin console. This is not to say that you should necessarily block “unauthorized” agents en masse. Your employees are learning to rely on them, and there’s great productivity improvement potential. 

Instead, treat the agent as an external entity. Someone else runs it, and the employee owns it. What you do have is the other end: the accounts, grants, and sessions it uses inside your systems.

For users, it’s good to have the agents run on a computer in the vendor’s cloud or on their own server. For you, it’s a headache, even if the vendor's architecture is thoughtful. Take Muse, which runs a dedicated VM with a guard called Sentinel that checks every outbound request, and tokens that the agent itself never handles. In other words, the Sentinel enforces the users’ policy rather than the employer's, and corporate session tokens end up on someone else’s computer. 

Local agents running on laptops have the opposite problem. Credentials stay local, but nothing tells the agent apart from the employee.

Enable the agent, govern the identity

So what’s the ideal solution? It looks something like this: employees can benefit from using their personal agent at work, but the workplace controls the reach via identities. 

It means: 

  • Discovering the agents already connected. This is your Shadow AI inventory, which you assemble based on the different ways AI agents access your systems. These can be OAuth grants to agent vendors, sign-ins from vendor cloud ranges, long-lived API keys issued to unknown clients, or EDR findings. 
  • Attributing each agent to a human owner.
  • Right-sizing the agent’s access. A personal agent inherits everything its owner can do, and it's usually asked to do a sliver of that. 
  • Retiring the agent when the owner leaves, including grants, tokens, and sessions that outlive the account.

Easier said than done, obviously, but some of the fundamentals are there. More will likely be added in the coming months to create the connective tissue between personal AI agents and workplaces. For example, we still need to know if whoever signs in with a username and password is an employee or their agent. Agent-to-agent communication isn’t solved yet. And the ability to compartmentalize knowledge, so that a personal agent loses it during offboarding, isn’t here yet.

Additional controls are coming, but you don’t have to wait for the vendors to catch up. Token Security already finds the personal agents connected to your systems, ties each one to its owner, trims its access, and shuts it off when the employee leaves. Identity is the control plane for AI agents and personal agents are no different. See it on your own environment.

  • AI Attacks Move at Machine Speed. Can Your Identity Security Keep Up? → AI-powered attacks can now move from reconnaissance to privilege escalation faster than traditional security teams can investigate and respond.   • AI Agents Have Too Much Access — Learn How to Control the Risk → AI agents are moving fast inside organizations, often with access to sensitive data, credentials, and business systems before security teams have full visibility or control. This webinar breaks down how shadow AI creates insider risk and shows how to govern AI access, reduce exposure, and enable safer adoption without slowing the business.

📰 Around the Cyber World

  • The India-nexus adversary known as Dropping Elephant (aka Patchwork) has been observed targeting government, defense, naval, aerospace/UAV, academic, and other strategically significant sectors across Pakistan, Sri Lanka, China, and South Korea. "The group continues to use spear-phishing campaigns with malicious LNK attachments to deliver PowerShell-based malware, DLL sideloading payloads, and in-memory RAT," Arctic Wolf said. 
  • Bitter, another threat actor assessed to be operating with interests aligned to India, targeted a European embassy in Asia in June 2026 with a spear-phishing email bearing a FIFA World Cup-themed lure to deliver BDarkRAT. "The attackers compromised a legitimate mailbox belonging to a diplomatic account from an African country to send the malicious message," Trellix said. "The attack utilized a multistage delivery method beginning with a ZIP file attachment containing a VHDX disk image. Inside this image lay a shortcut (.lnk) masquerading as a PDF document. This process established a scheduled task, deceptively named to appear like a system error to ensure persistence, and beaconed to a remote server. This initial connection facilitated reconnaissance by gathering system information and eventually downloading a second-stage MSI installer, which deployed the BDarkRAT remote-access trojan."
  • Let's Encrypt said TLS certificate lifetimes are dropping from 90 to 64 days by default starting February 2027, in preparation for 45-day lifetimes planned for 2028.
  • In a lengthy post on X, Microsoft's CEO Satya Nadella called out the dangers posed by highly advanced AI models, stating AI can no longer be treated as a "set of nested black boxes" and urged building a more transparent system where models can be contained, observed, and leave behind "tamper-proof human-readable evidence." Nadella added, "We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start. Think of it like an emergency brake.   • Data from Comparitech showed that Q3 2026 saw the highest quarterly figures to date for ransomware attacks, with 2,627 incidents reported in total. This represents a 29% increase from Q2 2026, when 2,030 attacks were recorded and a 61% increase from Q3 2025, when 1,636 attacks took place. The median ransomware demand was $150,000 and the average was $602,400. The most prolific gangs were Qilin and The Gentlemen.
  • Oleg Korniev, 42, a dual citizen of Ukraine and Russia, pleaded guilty in the U.S. to running a sophisticated international money laundering organization that laundered millions of dollars stolen from U.S. victims. The criminal organization recruited over 15,000 U.S.-based money mules to launder at least $10 million stolen by hackers from over 750 U.S. bank accounts. Korniev was one of the leaders of Your Mule Cashout (YMCO).
  • A U.S. jury convicted Jonathan Spalletta (aka Cthulhon and Jspalletta), 36, of Maryland, of computer fraud and money laundering over two separate hacks of decentralized crypto exchange Uranium Finance in 2021. He faces up to 10 years in prison on the fraud count and 20 years on the money laundering count. "In the first hack, on April 8, 2021, Spalletta engaged in a deceptive series of transactions with Uranium's smart contract that Spalletta used to withdraw far more 'rewards' in cryptocurrency than he was authorized to receive," the Justice Department said. "He repeated those transactions over and over until he had drained the liquidity pool of nearly all its rewards tokens. In total, Spalletta successfully extracted cryptocurrency worth approximately $1.4 million in the first hack. In the second hack, on April 28, 2021, Spalletta exploited an error in the Uranium smart contract that governed how much cryptocurrency he could withdraw in a liquidity pool on Uranium. Spalletta exploited that issue across multiple separate Uranium liquidity pools, fraudulently obtaining approximately $53.3 million in cryptocurrency and causing Uranium to shut down due to lack of funds." The stolen funds were eventually laundered through a complex series of cryptocurrency transactions, including by using the cryptocurrency mixer Tornado Cash.
  • OpenAI disclosed it disrupted two influence operations from Russia (Dark Clark) and Iran (Bogus Bylines) that used ChatGPT and other AI tools to create "false front" entities, such as seven fake journalist personas and covert think tanks, that successfully planted stories and narratives in mainstream news publications. "They used those entities to launder geopolitical, conflict-related messaging into their target audiences," OpenAI said. "Both operations were multi-dimensional, trying a range of different tactics to achieve their goals. As well as long-form articles, the Iranian operation generated batches of social media comments, generally on topics related to the US-Iran war. As well as controlling the 'think tank,' the Russian operation created fake 'leaked' documents and audio scripts, some of which we identified as being spread online." Some of the outlets that published the articles, however, had substantial audiences, including one with 2 million Facebook followers.
  • Threat actors are embedding "AI-Analysis Evasion" (aka A3) capabilities in malware by embedding natural-language instructions to influence automated analysis. Such techniques have been detected against four malware families: FRUITSHELL, PLOTSAFE, HOLLOWCLAD, and MANTLEMAZE, per Cisco Talos. This includes anti-analysis comments in source code, in some cases generating them from a template and incorporating intimidation notes that instruct the model that it is a monitored honeypot. "What began as a direct-instruction technique has evolved to target multiple models through template spraying," Talos said. "Malware authors are also attempting to establish multiple analysis-bypass conditions by using direct or indirect deterrence instructions aimed at the model."
  • A brand deal scam is targeting YouTube creators by impersonating Hollyland, a legitimate manufacturer of wireless transmission and audiovisual equipment. The phishing emails lead to a fake website that instructs them to sign in with their Google account with an aim to harvest their credentials. "The attackers who hijack your account could use it to access other linked services or impersonate them to contact your followers or collaborators," ESET said. "The compromised account can also be misused to spread malicious links and peddle other scams."
  • A high-severity flaw in NVIDIA's DCGM Exporter GPU monitoring tool (CVE-2026-47483, CVSS score: 8.2) could be abused by unauthenticated attackers to flood its profiling endpoints with concurrent unauthenticated requests to exhaust resources and crash the service, potentially slowing AI workloads running on the same host. Lava Security said it found roughly 2,100 hosts exposing the exporter to the internet without authentication between March and May 2026, leaking telemetry data from more than 12,000 GPUs. The hosts belonged to about 300 organizations, with the GPUs representing about $100 million in hardware. The flaw has been addressed in version 4.8.2 or later. "As AI infrastructure scales, organizations need to protect every layer of the stack and know exactly what they are responsible for versus what their provider is responsible for," Lava said.
  • Raheim Hamilton, 30, a Virginia man who co-created and operated Empire Market, a dark web marketplace that peddled illegal goods and services, was sentenced to 40 years in federal prison. Raheim pleaded guilty in January 2026.
  • Three new malware loaders have been spotted in the wild: 2CLoader, which delivers Vidar, Remus Stealer, and XWorm RAT, AvisLoader, which is delivered via ClickFix lures and communicates via Fox, an encrypted peer-to-peer (P2P) messaging network, to fetch commands and additional payloads from the operator, and Sauron Loader, which offers loader-type functionality exclusively to Russian-speaking cybercriminals.
  • Details have emerged about two Zammad flaws that were exploited as zero-days to breach the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD). According to Horizon3.ai and Sysdig, CVE-2026-102489 is a remote code execution flaw affecting versions 6.3.0 to 6.5.4, while CVE-2026-102490 is a local privilege escalation (LPE) flaw affecting all versions from 1.5.0 to 7.1.0-alpha. On October 2, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by October 5, 2026.
  • An investigation into a September 2026 Akira ransomware attack undertaken by Huntress found that "the threat actor behind the attack accessed the endpoint via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), disabled antivirus, and deployed Rclone for data exfiltration, before deploying the ransomware. The actor also deployed a GOST tunneling tool, likely for persistence."

Conclusion

A few arrests and takedowns brought some good news this week. But the bigger picture is less comforting. Attackers keep finding new ways in, old mistakes still work, and even the systems meant to help or protect people aren't always what they seem.

That's it for this edition. Not every story here needs your attention, but a few might deserve a closer look. Especially the ones that sound a little too familiar to your own setup. Better to spot the problem in someone else's story than become part of the next one. See you next week.

Conclusion

A few arrests and takedowns brought some good news this week. But the bigger picture is less comforting. Attackers keep finding new ways in, old mistakes still work, and even the systems meant to help or protect people aren't always what they seem.

That's it for this edition. Not every story here needs your attention, but a few might deserve a closer look. Especially the ones that sound a little too familiar to your own setup. Better to spot the problem in someone else's story than become part of the next one. See you next week.

item.title: Low-Cost Android Phones Ship With Preinstalled Malware That Turns Them Into Residential Proxies (2026)
item.description:
Low-cost Android smartphones have been shipped with malicious software baked into the device firmware, allowing bad actors to covertly install apps, conduct ad fraud, and turn devices into residential proxies.

The activity, which targets Android devices built on MediaTek platforms across several brands, is being tracked by Bitdefender under the moniker Midnight Mimosa.

The preinstalled malware ("com.android.system.lite") runs with system-level privileges, which make it possible to install or uninstall a rotating set of at least 32 disguised apps, grant itself additional permissions to accessibility services, notifications, and SMS, and load arbitrary code supplied remotely by the operators.

Specifically, it fetches a remote configuration from an external server and then downloads and executes additional payloads designed to conduct ad fraud and silent installation or removal of partner apps. These apps incorporate proxyware, ad fraud, and code execution features. It can also grant permission to any Android app package.

"This essentially means its operators could install and delete apps at will, tuning each device to their needs, including making them part of large botnets," the Romanian cybersecurity company said.

"This scheme is likely designed mainly to generate revenue. The operators carry out ad and click fraud, collect device and installed-app information, and turn infected devices into residential-proxy relay nodes, making them zombies in botnets."

It's worth emphasizing that the malware itself doesn't engage in fraudulent clicks. Instead, the monetization effort is driven by dropper apps that masquerade as seemingly harmless utility apps, which are responsible for loading genuine ads through a legitimate advertising software development kit (SDK). The end goal is to load an invisible window on top of apps that registers the ads being shown.

In all, Bitdefender said it discovered 13 apps on Google Play that communicate with the same servers that control the malware, indicating the campaign is not limited to preinstalled firmware. Unlike the preinstalled malware, the Play Store apps provide genuine functionality, such as weather information or QR-code scanning. But they also load and display ads outside the apps, including when a user is not actively using the phone.

The names of the apps are listed below. None of them are currently available for download from the Play Store -

  • Wavrge (com.audify.editor.wavrge)
  • App Icon DIY (appicon.diy.tools.prop)
  • Audify (com.audify.editor.pro)
  • QR Pocket (com.prorestore.qr)
  • All Deleted Messages Recovery (com.message.recovery.prorestore)
  • WeatherGo (com.go.weather.mot)
  • CoolWeather (com.cool.weather.yl)
  • Daily Weather (com.dmstudio.weather)
  • Lock & Hide (com.dl.guard.lock)
  • QuickText Extractor (picturetranslate.extractor.text.lite)
  • NoteMaster (com.notemaster.record.mark)
  • Tap to Translate (com.arabmusic.tap.aghani_tamerhosny)
  • Tasky (org.life.goal.tools)

A notable aspect of the malware is that it disables the Google Play Store app prior to installing a payload app, likely in an attempt to bypass Play Protect safeguards, and then re-enable the app after the payload is run. 

What's more, the malware has been detected on devices with firmware signed using certificates attributed to Shenzhen Zediel Co., Ltd, a Chinese Android device manufacturer. However, it's unclear at this stage if the certificate owner was involved in or aware of the malware deployment. However, Bitdefender noted that it also detected other company names over the course of its investigation.

The preinstalled nature of the malware suggests a compromise of the device supply chain, with Bitdefender highlighting some level of infrastructure overlaps with Android.Phantom, which was documented by Doctor Web in January 2026 as bundled within modded games and popular apps to conduct click fraud.

The vast majority of the infected devices are located in Mexico, followed by France, Italy, the U.S., Germany, Brazil, Spain, the U.K., Canada, Romania, Poland, and Thailand. Collectively, the campaign has been observed on thousands of unique devices across more than 150 countries over roughly two years. Many of the impacted phones appear to be low-cost, white-label or counterfeit devices, including models that borrow the names of better-known Samsung Galaxy phones and even Apple iPhones.

This is not the first time a firmware-level backdoor has been observed targeting Android devices. Late last year, Kaspersky disclosed details of another malware codenamed Keenadu that was discovered preinstalled on certain models of tablets running Android to primarily enable ad fraud.

"Preinstalled malware is a different threat class," Bitdefender said. "Every user-facing defense assumes the owner is in the loop at installation: the install prompt, the store review, Play Protect, and the ability to uninstall afterwards."

"Remediation cannot rely on uninstall. Because the root component ships in the system partition, an affected owner cannot remove it by the normal route. Clearing the device requires firmware-level cleanup or disabling the component over ADB, and neither is realistic for most people who own these phones. The durable fix sits with the vendors and the marketplaces that ship and sell the affected firmware."

item.title: GitLab Patches CVSS 10.0 Flaw That Could Let Unauthenticated Users Run Server Code (2026)
item.description:
GitLab has released patches for a maximum-severity security flaw impacting its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) software that could result in arbitrary code execution.

"GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation," the company said in a Monday advisory.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97229, has been described as an integer overflow issue. It carries a CVSS score of 10.0. It affects the following versions -

  • All versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8
  • All versions from 19.3 before 19.3.5, and
  • All versions from 19.4 before 19.4.2

Patches for the flaw are available in versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8. Also addressed are three high-severity bugs -

  • CVE-2026-92883 (CVSS score: 8.7) - A cross-site scripting vulnerability that could allow an authenticated user to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of other users' browser sessions via a specially crafted repository.
  • CVE-2026-16301 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper authorization vulnerability in the downstream pipeline creation service that could allow an authenticated user with Developer role to execute CI/CD pipelines on protected branches.
  • CVE-2026-14814 (CVSS score: 8.2) - A permissive regular expression vulnerability that could allow a user to poison cached responses for raw repository files, causing targeted users’ CI/CD pipelines to execute specially crafted content and potentially exposing protected environment variables.

The disclosure comes weeks after it remediated a critical flaw in AI Gateway (CVE-2026-90970, CVSS score: 9.9) that could have allowed an authenticated user with Duo Agent Platform access to break out of the prompt template sandbox via a specially crafted flow configuration and achieve arbitrary command execution on the AI Gateway.

Last month, another maximum-severity security flaw in GitLab CE and EE (CVE-2026-85706, CVSS score: 10.0) witnessed in-the-wild probes within hours of public disclosure.

item.title: Two Critical MarkLogic Flaws Could Give Delegated Managers Persistent Admin Control (2026)
item.description:
Two of 31 newly disclosed flaws in Progress Software's MarkLogic Server database could let an account given only some management privileges take administrator control of the server, the company says.

Progress published all 31 on October 12 and scored five of them critical. Fixes have been available since September 10, in MarkLogic 11.3.7 and MarkLogic 12.1.0.

Affected releases, and the release that fixes each:

  • MarkLogic 11.x before 11.3.7: upgrade to 11.3.7
  • MarkLogic 12.x before 12.1.0: upgrade to 12.1.0

MarkLogic 11.3 is the long-term support (LTS) line. The 12 line, which Progress calls an innovation release, has no patched 12.0 release. Its fix is 12.1.0, which also adds new features.

Installing the fixes for the 10 MarkLogic flaws Progress disclosed in August is not enough. Those fixes arrived in 11.3.6 and 12.0.3, and both releases are affected by the new flaws.

Progress's CVE records and its upgrade notes for the two releases do not say whether any of the 31 flaws has been used in attacks. None was in the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog when The Hacker News checked on October 13.

The same records and notes list no workaround for customers who cannot upgrade yet.

What the Critical Flaws Allow

Progress scored three of the five critical flaws 9.9 out of 10 on the CVSS scale and the other two 9.6. For each one, the attacker must already have a privilege or a way to run code on the server, according to the company's CVE records.

Two of them involve forests. In MarkLogic, a forest is a collection of documents that is attached to a database.

CVE Score What the Attacker Needs What It Could Allow
CVE-2026-85947 9.9 Forest-management privileges Create a persistent administrator account, potentially giving complete administrative control of the server
CVE-2026-85948 9.9 Manage-user-level privileges Gain persistent administrative control, through an XQuery injection flaw in a deprecated Management API path
CVE-2026-85955 9.9 Query-execution access and the xdmp-eval-in privilege Run server-side code with elevated permissions
CVE-2026-85956 9.6 Delegated database-administrator privileges Back up or restore forests outside its own database, allowing access to or changes to what Progress calls "security-critical data"
CVE-2026-9191 9.6 The ability to run code through certain REST and XDBC evaluation paths Perform unauthorized actions or compromise an authenticated session

The fix for CVE-2026-85947 shows which accounts are at issue. A "forest-scoped administrative grant" is no longer enough on its own to attach a forest to a database of the account's choosing, the upgrade notes say. They also tell customers to review delegated forest and database privilege assignments before upgrading, and to audit the roles that hold xdmp-eval-in.

Outside researchers reported four of the five through Bugcrowd. A researcher using the handle rexnets is credited with CVE-2026-85947, CVE-2026-85948, and CVE-2026-85956, and another using the handle WaltWhitehat is credited with CVE-2026-9191.

Flaws That Depend on Configuration

Progress scored 24 of the remaining flaws high and two medium. The highest, CVE-2026-85954, at 8.6, could allow an attacker to gain more privileges than granted by passing values to certain XQuery functions.

Several of the others apply only where a named feature or platform is in use:

  • SAML: In deployments that use SAML authentication, an unauthenticated remote attacker could make the server accept an assertion it should reject (CVE-2026-85962). On 11.x, the SAML parser could also process external DTDs or entities (CVE-2026-85957).
  • OAuth: An attacker could use a token that the server should not accept (CVE-2026-85958). The fix adds issuer and audience checks for Ping Identity and other OAuth configurations.
  • Password-based Kerberos: In certain configurations, an attacker positioned on the network could impersonate the Kerberos authentication service (CVE-2026-85972).
  • Cloud hosting: An authenticated attacker could access internal cloud services and obtain cloud credentials on Azure (CVE-2026-85951) and on Linux-based cloud deployments (CVE-2026-85952).
  • Diagnostic logs: Under certain configurations, the server could write security-sensitive information to diagnostic logs (CVE-2026-85949 and, on Azure, CVE-2026-85961). AWS secret keys and session tokens were written in plaintext when the affected IAM trace path was enabled, the upgrade notes say.
  • Amazon S3: Connections to S3 could use cleartext by default (CVE-2026-85975).
  • Query Console: A remote attacker who gets a logged-in Query Console user to open a malicious page could run server-side code with that user's permissions (CVE-2026-85960). An authenticated Query Console user could read arbitrary server files (CVE-2026-85964).
  • Legacy components: OpsDirector, a deprecated feature, could let an unauthenticated remote attacker make requests to internal services or forge trusted requests (CVE-2026-85963). Legacy InfoStudio modules could give access to server files (CVE-2026-85953).

The rest include three memory-safety flaws, a cross-site scripting flaw, HTTP response splitting in Query Console, inconsistent TLS hostname checks on some outbound connections, and cleartext cluster-management traffic on 12.x.

What the Upgrade Changes

Progress tells customers to read its upgrade notes, the known incompatibilities for 11.3.7 and those for 12.1.0, before upgrading. The 11.3.7 notes list behavior changes tied to 22 of the flaws, and the 12.1.0 notes to 21.

Changes that can break existing code, tools, or automation include:

item.title: Attackers Heat French Supermarket Fridges Up to 50°C by Hijacking Danfoss Controllers (2026)
item.description:
Attackers took remote control of fridges and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets on the night of October 11 and warmed them, forcing stores to throw food away, several retail chains said.

The attackers reached them through the controller that runs all of a store's fridges and freezers, a device made by Danish company Danfoss that maintenance firms can manage remotely. Les Mousquetaires, which owns the Intermarché chain, said its fridges and freezers were put into defrost and heated to as much as 50°C.

CERT-FR, the French government's computer emergency response team, said in an alert published in French on October 12 that it is aware of numerous compromises affecting two Danfoss controller series, the AK-SM and the AK-SC. It told operators to disconnect the controllers or filter access to them.

CERT-FR is part of ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency. ANSSI's head, Vincent Strubel, called it urgent to take the two series off the internet or filter access very tightly, AFP reported.

Neither French authorities nor Danfoss has so far said who carried out the attack or how the attackers got into the controllers. Danfoss said most of the units hit were older models that it no longer updates.

Which Chains Were Hit

The chains gave their own figures to AFP, Reuters and broadcaster RTL. Each counts the stores the attack reached.

Retailer Stores Reported Hit Source
Intermarché and Netto (Les Mousquetaires) At least 300 across both brands, per AFP. About 150 stores, per Reuters Company statements, October 12
Coopérative U 80 of 2,000 Chief executive Dominique Schelcher, on RTL, October 13
Carrefour 80 supermarkets Company statements to AFP and Reuters, October 12
Monoprix About 30 Company statement to AFP, October 12
E.Leclerc Several stores Company statement to AFP, October 12

A store on that list did not always lose its stock. Schelcher told RTL that the cold chain held in most of the 80 Coopérative U stores hit, and that only a minority could not react fast enough and lost goods, according to AFP. He praised the quick reaction of store staff and refrigeration contractors.

Intermarché, by contrast, said its affected stores had to throw away all the products concerned.

Thierry Cotillard, who heads Les Mousquetaires, told broadcaster BFMTV he expected losses of tens of millions of euros across France, according to Reuters.

In its statements on October 12, Danfoss gave no figure for how many systems were hit. It told Reuters it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems."

Which Controllers, and Whether They Can Be Patched

Danfoss told AFP that most of the units hit were older products that no longer get software or security updates, and it named two: the AK-SM 800 and the AK-SC 355.

Danfoss declared the AK-SM 800 end-of-life in May 2021 and phased out the AK-SC 355 in 2016. In an October 2025 newsletter, it said it would end all services for such older products and urged customers to plan replacements.

Some units of the current model, the AK-SM 800A, were also hit. Those were running outdated firmware, according to Danfoss's statement to trade publication Cooling Post, which did not name the versions.

Controller Status, According to Danfoss Advice From CERT-FR and Danfoss
AK-SM 800 End of life since May 2021. No software or security updates Disconnect it or filter access. Danfoss urges replacement
AK-SC 355 Phased out in 2016. No software or security updates Disconnect it or filter access. Danfoss urges replacement
AK-SM 800A Current model. Package 5.3.x, dated October 2026, was the latest listed on October 13 Disconnect it or filter access. Danfoss advises keeping firmware up to date

As of October 13, Danfoss's security advisories page listed no advisory about the attack or about either older model.

What Operators Should Do

CERT-FR's first instruction covers every AK-SM and AK-SC controller: disconnect it or filter access to it. Exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice, the alert says.

Where remote administration cannot be avoided, limiting access to trusted IP addresses is a first, temporary step. Beyond that, the alert advises following CERT-FR's hardening recommendations, which were written for the energy and water sector.

Where a controller may have been compromised, the alert lists six steps, in this order:

  1. Limit network access to the controllers to service providers only.
  2. Do a factory reset.
  3. Apply all available security fixes.
  4. Change the device's secrets, such as passwords.
  5. Check the existing accounts.
  6. Reconfigure the device completely.

Danfoss no longer issues fixes for the AK-SM 800 and the AK-SC 355, so the third step offers their owners no new fix.

For the AK-SM 800A, the latest software package Danfoss listed on October 13 was 5.3.x. A system on version 3.x should move to 4.x first, and a controller cannot be downgraded once it runs 5.3.x, according to the package's readme.

Starting with version 4.0, a setting called Strict Session Control is enabled by default and makes HTTPS mandatory. Danfoss's pages do not say whether the 5.3.x package was released in response to the attack.

Danfoss told Cooling Post it was working with customers on "firmware updates where available, stronger network protections and removing direct internet exposure where applicable."

Its general security guidance, published in French, also tells operators to keep controllers unreachable from the internet, change default passwords when a system is installed, and require remote users to log in through a single managed entry point.

CERT-FR had published no indicators of compromise as of October 13, so operators have no official signs to check for.

Coopérative U's stores do not buy directly from Danfoss. They are customers of refrigeration contractors that supply them with the Danfoss system, Schelcher said.

How the Attackers Got In Is Not Established

As of October 13, CERT-FR had named no vulnerability, no firmware version, and no way in. Its alert warns against exposing management interfaces to the internet without saying that was the route.

A person close to French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu told AFP that ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and had contacted the vendor. No CVE was named, and the statement does not say the vulnerability was used in the attack.

E.Leclerc told AFP that a cyberattack had affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers, with effects on cold equipment in several of its stores. The supplier was not named.

Danfoss issued fixes for three flaws in the newer AK-SM 800A in 2025. Neither French authorities nor Danfoss has linked them to this attack.

CVE-2025-41450 is an authentication bypass, a way past the login, in versions before 4.2. CVE-2025-41451 is a command injection flaw that could lead to remote code execution, and CVE-2025-41452 could allow a denial-of-service attack. Both need a login and were fixed in version 4.3.1.

Researchers at Claroty described the three flaws in August, said they could be combined into attack chains, and reported finding thousands of AK-SM 800A management interfaces reachable from the internet. Their tests of the flaws were laboratory work on the newer model. The report describes no attacks and does not mention the two older models.

Danfoss's October 2025 newsletter records earlier attacks on the AK-SM 800: 16 Russian supermarkets using the model were targeted in 2022, and 40 Israeli stores were hacked the same year. All 40 lacked proper firewall or VPN protection, and the newsletter names no vulnerability in either case.

The Inquiry and Reports From Other Countries

The Paris prosecutor's office has opened an inquiry on its own initiative, it told AFP. Its cybercrime section leads the inquiry, which is assigned to the anti-cybercrime office known as OFAC.

The inquiry is to count the victims and establish the link between the attack and the damage they reported, which includes lost food and equipment that began to catch fire.

ANSSI is in contact with cybersecurity agencies in other European countries because those countries may be affected, the person close to the Prime Minister said.

Félix Aimé, a senior threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia, told Reuters that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected. Reuters gave no details on those cases.

item.title: Product Walkthrough: Bitdefender AI Visibility and Control (2026)
item.description:
A user opens a browser tab, pastes data into a chat assistant, and nothing is installed.

A developer adds a coding assistant as an editor extension, and nothing shows up in the installed programs list.

Someone downloads a local model runtime, a program that runs models directly on the machine instead of sending data to an external service, because they were told not to send company data outside.

None of this reaches your software inventory. Tasked with controlling AI, an administrator often resorts to blocking well-known AI websites and taking enforcement action without knowing what is actually running.

Bitdefender GravityZone AI Visibility and Control (AIVC) is the discovery and risk layer that answers the questions you have, first: Which AI software is present on your protected Windows endpoints, who is running it, and how much risk does each one carry.

What Your Software Inventory Was Never Built to Watch

AI Visibility and Control covers four classes of exposure, and each one sits outside a control you already own.

  • AI services reached through the browser. Hosted assistants are the path most organizations already worry about. The inventory identifies which services are running, on which machines, and whether you have marked them as approved. A service with no findings is not automatically approved; a clean result on a tool your organization never sanctioned is still shadow AI. This ensures filtering decisions are based on real user activity rather than hand-picked domain lists.
  • AI inside the development environment. Coding assistants run inside editors that already hold source repositories, and often credentials and configuration files in the same working directory. They are rarely covered by whatever you decided about chat assistants, because nobody classified them as the same kind of tool.
  • AI running locally on the endpoint. Local model runtimes, MCP servers, and agent frameworks execute on the machine itself. A control that governs which websites an endpoint may reach does not see them at all. The MCP server is the sharpest case: its entire purpose is to hand a model access to something else, and it usually arrives as a configuration entry rather than as an install.
  • AI with reach into other systems. Where a tool is configured to connect to a database, a code repository, an internal API, or a third-party model service, that connection is part of your attack surface. AI Visibility and Control records the configured scope of those connections, not the data moving across them.

How AIVC Finds and Categorizes What It Finds

GravityZone AI Visibility and Control discovery takes place during the risk scan. The GravityZone BEST agent collects metadata from each endpoint and keeps that collection minimized: it records what AI software is present and how it is configured, not what anyone does with it. AIVC does not inspect prompts, chat history, model weights, credentials, or full file content.

AI Visibility and Control recognizes more than 50 AI agents and more than 70,000 skills, the modular code packages that extend an agent's capabilities and that arrive from public registries. Because agents exercise permissions through these skills, considering only agents while ignoring skills would account for only a fraction of the total exposure.

Every discovered service is assigned to one of 17 functional categories based on its primary function (e.g., LLMs, coding, productivity, and others). The category makes the inventory actionable at the policy level because it maps to the question the reviewer arrived with. A security team investigating data-handling risk, filters to LLMs and chatbots plus Platforms and infrastructure. A development manager auditing what touches source code goes straight to Coding and Tools and skills. A governance review covering automation risk works from Agents, Automation, and MCP.

Two Views, and a Connector Nobody Installed

AI Visibility and Control appears in Bitdefender GravityZone Console as two views, each answering a different question.

AI Services answers "what AI is running in my environment?" It is the inventory: every discovered service with its risk score. item.title: LG Smart TVs Vulnerable to Pre-Auth Root Takeover From Local Network (2026)
item.description:
Three vulnerabilities in LG's webOS can be chained to give an attacker on the same local network root access to certain smart TVs without a PIN or any interaction from the owner.

LG has issued a fix, according to an advisory published by SSD Secure Disclosure on October 12.

The chain was tested on two TV models, the 32LQ636BPSA and the 27TQ600SW, running webOS 7.5.7-25 on firmware 04.54.40. Whether other models or firmware versions are affected is not known.

Owners of affected TVs should check for a firmware update. No workaround is available for those who cannot update yet.

The attack enters through a service that the TV exposes on port 3001, which is used by the LG ThinQ app for pairing. An attacker replays a manifest from sync-demo, a built-in app already on the device, signed with a test certificate the firmware trusts. A permission in the manifest causes the pairing service to skip the PIN prompt and hand over a privileged key.

With that key, the attacker launches another built-in app, cmp-client, and points it to an attacker-controlled page. The app does not check where it navigates, and the loaded page keeps access to PalmServiceBridge, an internal interface to the TV's system services.

Through that bridge, the attacker calls the system logging service, pmlogd, passing shell commands through an input field the service does not check. Because pmlogd runs as root, the injected command runs as root.

This is not the first time the local network attack surface has led to root access on LG smart TVs. In 2024, Bitdefender disclosed a different set of webOS vulnerabilities that also allowed unauthenticated access from the network, affected different components, and were patched in March 2024. A separate chain demonstrated at TyphoonPWN 2025 used a path traversal on a different port.

The chain was demonstrated by an anonymous researcher who won third place in the LG webOS category at TyphoonPWN 2026, held in Seoul in May. No CVE identifiers have been assigned, and no exploitation in the wild has been reported.

item.title: [Webinar] How to Stop AI-Driven Privilege Escalation With Runtime Identity Controls (2026)
item.description:
The dangerous part of a stolen identity isn't always the initial login. It's what an attacker can do with that access next.

With AI accelerating reconnaissance, exploitation of vulnerabilities, and privilege escalation, attackers can move through systems faster than security teams can investigate. A compromised account that looks legitimate at first could become the starting point for a much larger attack.

And that's where traditional identity security faces a serious problem: Checking who gets access isn't enough if you can't control what happens after.

See How to Stop AI-Powered Identity Attacks — Register for the Webinar

Why Traditional Identity Controls Are Falling Behind

Many identity security controls focus on authentication, permissions, and access policies. But what happens when a trusted identity is compromised, its behavior changes, or an attacker begins exploiting already granted privileges?

That gap becomes more dangerous as AI-powered attacks accelerate.

Attackers can automate parts of the attack chain while defenders are still collecting alerts, investigating activity, and deciding how to respond.

The answer isn't simply detecting attacks faster. It's the ability to evaluate and control access in real time while an identity is actively being used.

This is the idea behind runtime identity security.

In this upcoming expert-led webinar, you'll learn:

  • Where attackers find identity gaps across cloud, on-premises, SaaS, and AI environments.
  • Why AI-powered attacks challenge traditional defenses and reduce the time available to respond.
  • How runtime identity security works to evaluate access continuously and enforce security decisions when they matter.
  • How to prepare your defenses for AI-driven attacks that move at machine speed.

The Next Identity Attack May Not Give You Time to React

If attackers can compromise identities and escalate privileges in minutes, discovering suspicious activity after the fact may already be too late.

Security teams need to know not just who has access, but whether that access should still be trusted right now.

This session explores how to close that gap and build an identity security strategy designed to keep pace with the speed of modern attacks.

item.title: Xandr Fined a Record €8.6 Million for Relaying Grindr Data Revealing Sexual Orientation (2026)
item.description:
The Norwegian Data Protection Authority (DPA) has fined Xandr, an advertising unit owned by Microsoft, €8.6 million ($9.62 million) for illegally relaying ​Grindr users' sensitive data to advertisers.

The administrative penalty is the largest issued by the data protection watchdog, arguing the case merited a high fine because of the "very serious" nature of the breach. The infringements occurred between July 2018 and April 2020.

"Xandr acted as an intermediary that relayed the personal data of Grindr users in Norway, including data revealing sexual orientation, to potentially thousands of other companies," the Data Protection Authority said in a statement.

The data protection authority said its investigation found that Xandr was a joint controller with Grindr, which meant it was responsible for obtaining users' consent before processing their data.

Instead of ensuring they had the legal basis for their own processing of the data, Xandr pointed fingers at Grindr, stating it assumed the online dating app had collected users' consent to do so," it added.

Xandr was formed by AT&T following its June 2018 acquisition of AppNexus. The name is a reference to Alexander Graham Bell, who founded AT&T in 1885. It was subsequently sold to Microsoft in late December 2021, following which the brand was retired and consolidated under the Microsoft Ads umbrella in June 2023.

The case dates back to 2020, when the country's consumer council, along with Austrian privacy non-profit None of Your Business (noyb), filed a complaint against Xandr, accusing it of unlawfully sharing users' personal data for commercial purposes without getting users' explicit consent. Thousands of users in Norway are said to have been subjected to unlawful sharing of their sensitive data as a result of this practice.

"The essence of the infringement was Xandr's participation in so-called real-time bidding, where they acted both on the buyer and seller side," the watchdog said. "When a person opened Grindr, their personal data was in many cases relayed through Xandr to potentially thousands of actors in the advertising ecosystem."

"Advertisers could thereby bid against each other to present targeted adverts, completely hidden from the individual user."

The DPA also said the fine was calculated taking into account Xandr's total annual turnover during the two-year time period, which predates Microsoft's acquisition. Xandr has three weeks to appeal the decision.

Responding to the DPA's decision, noyb described the fine as a "major blow for the online advertising and commercial surveillance industry" and said that "companies such as Xandr are eventually held accountable for their shady practices."

In a statement shared with Reuters, Microsoft said it's reviewing the decision and assessing its options.

Last month, Grindr opted to pay £26 million ($35.1 million) to settle a lawsuit in the U.K. over allegations that it shared users' personal information, including their HIV status, with third-parties.

The development comes as a Texas federal judge granted final approval of a $177 million AT&T settlement for classes of AT&T consumers whose personal information was exposed in two separate data breaches that took place in March and July 2024. The class-action lawsuit was settled in November 2025.

The March 2024 incident involved the publication of a dataset on the dark web containing Social Security numbers. It affected about 7.6 million current AT&T account holders and approximately 65.4 million former account holders, the telecom service provider noted at the time.

The second hack revolved around threat actors illegally downloading AT&T customer data from a third-party cloud platform hosted by Snowflake. The American company said that calls and text message records that occurred between May 1 and October 31, 2022 were compromised for "nearly all" cellular customers.

item.title: GitHub Tightens npm Publishing After Flaw Left 1,500+ Packages Vulnerable to Hijacking (2026)
item.description:
GitHub has taken the step of expiring unvalidated npm trusted publishing configurations 48 hours after creation after researchers found that it was possible for an attacker to push new versions of a different user's package without having to steal their credentials.

"Your configuration becomes validated and exempt from expiry after its first successful publish," the Microsoft-owned subsidiary said. "Changing the repository or project identity requires a new trust relationship with a fresh 48-hour validation window -- ordinary edits don't restart the deadline."

The change contains the risk associated with trusting a repository or project name that changes ownership, GitHub said, adding npm also rejects trusted publishing tokens from GitHub Actions issue_comment events going forward, along with the Existing pull_request_target restriction.

In an update to its documentation, GitHub states that a newly created trusted publisher configuration must complete its first successful publish within two days, which validates the configuration and binds it to the "repository's immutable identity."

The development comes in response to findings from Bloom Security, which discovered a loophole within npm's trusted publishing to take over thousands of packages and trigger a Shai-Hulud-style cascading supply chain attack. The findings were reported to GitHub on June 6, 2026.

"Imagine this: an attacker compromises a single package. An AI agent on a popular package maintainer's device autonomously pulls it for a project," security researcher Golan Myers said. "That single endpoint is used to push malicious code to the popular package. All the package users are exposed. All because one person with the correct access was exposed."

Trusted publishing was introduced in npm in July 2025 as a credential-free authentication method that allows developers to push npm packages from a CI/CD platform, such as GitHub Actions, using OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens.

When trusted publishing is configured, the developer's CI/CD provider generates a short-lived cryptographic token for a specific workflow run that the npm registry verifies against a pre-authorized configuration.

This eliminates the need to store, rotate, or manually manage long-lived npm secrets, reducing the risk of credential leaks. It also automatically generates provenance attestations for npm packages, allowing users to establish where a package was built and who published it, thereby strengthening software supply chain security.

However, as Bloom Security found, this security architecture suffered from a problem in how it identified that repository, also called a slug (i.e, the combination of the owner or organization and the repository name that's formatted as "owner/repository").

"It records the repository's address, [...] instead of the permanent ID GitHub assigns it, at least until a version is first published from that repository," Myers explained. "It is like a lock that checks the address on the door rather than who owns the house: when the owner moves out, whoever moves in gets the key."

Put differently, the numeric IDs that survive through repository renaming and transfers are carried by GitHub's OIDC tokens, but are completely ignored by npm until the first successful publish from that repository.

This means the trust is anchored to a name as opposed to an immutable repository ID, a loophole that can be abused by claiming abandoned slugs to inherit their trust. For this attack to succeed, the only prerequisite is that the victim's trusted publisher points to a GitHub slug an attacker can claim, and the repository has never been used to publish a version of the package to npm.

Once such a slug becomes available for use after a maintainer renames, transfers, or deletes a repository, an attacker can follow the steps below -

  • Create a repository at the freed slug at the "owner/repository" path, which causes GitHub to issue a fresh repository ID.
  • Create and trigger an npm publish workflow, which mints an OIDC token carrying the reclaimed slug and the new numeric repository ID
  • Submit the token to the npm exchange endpoint. Npm finds that the repository claim matches the stored slug and issues a publish credential.
  • The attacker receives a time-limited publish token for a package they do not own and pushes malicious changes to the registry.

An attack of this kind, codenamed SlugFest, can be abused to publish a new "malicious" version of the victim package under the legitimate package name, while inheriting existing reputation, download counts, and dependent relationships. This, in turn, can lead to supply chain attacks at scale.

AI agents running on developer machines can further compound the risk. "Agents resolve dependencies on their own, tend to take the latest version, and rarely check where a package came from," Bloom Security said. "A malicious version published through a reclaimed slug gets pulled in and runs with no human-in-the-loop."

The cybersecurity company said it found over 1,500 vulnerable packages that have been collectively downloaded more than 10 million times.

Developers who maintain npm packages are advised to perform the following actions -

  • Audit trusted publisher bindings and verify if the listed repository slug still resolves to the repository under their control.
  • If the repository has been renamed or transferred, delete the existing trust binding and re-create it pointing at the current slug.
  • Monitor for unexpected npm publish events.
  • Delete trust bindings every time a repository is deleted, transferred, or renamed.

"The attack requires no insider knowledge, no credential theft, and no race condition," Myers said. "The only precondition is slug availability (on a binding that has not yet been used to publish), which is entirely a function of the victim's own repository hygiene."

"What this research demonstrates is something the security community has seen repeatedly across supply chain attacks: the binding between a human-readable identifier and the thing it identifies is the most important invariant in any trust system. When that binding can be silently replaced – by the ordinary act of renaming a repository, not by any attacker action – the trust guarantee collapses."

This is not the first time unconventional supply chain attack vectors have been discovered. Earlier this August, Bloom Security also found that both Open VSX and Microsoft's VS Code Marketplace allowed extension packs to reference non-existent extensions in the marketplaces.
