GitHub has taken the step of expiring unvalidated npm trusted publishing configurations 48 hours after creation after researchers found that it was possible for an attacker to push new versions of a different user's package without having to steal their credentials.

"Your configuration becomes validated and exempt from expiry after its first successful publish," the Microsoft-owned subsidiary said. "Changing the repository or project identity requires a new trust relationship with a fresh 48-hour validation window -- ordinary edits don't restart the deadline."

The change contains the risk associated with trusting a repository or project name that changes ownership, GitHub said, adding npm also rejects trusted publishing tokens from GitHub Actions issue_comment events going forward, along with the Existing pull_request_target restriction.

In an update to its documentation, GitHub states that a newly created trusted publisher configuration must complete its first successful publish within two days, which validates the configuration and binds it to the "repository's immutable identity."

The development comes in response to findings from Bloom Security, which discovered a loophole within npm's trusted publishing to take over thousands of packages and trigger a Shai-Hulud-style cascading supply chain attack. The findings were reported to GitHub on June 6, 2026.

"Imagine this: an attacker compromises a single package. An AI agent on a popular package maintainer's device autonomously pulls it for a project," security researcher Golan Myers said. "That single endpoint is used to push malicious code to the popular package. All the package users are exposed. All because one person with the correct access was exposed."

Trusted publishing was introduced in npm in July 2025 as a credential-free authentication method that allows developers to push npm packages from a CI/CD platform, such as GitHub Actions, using OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens.

When trusted publishing is configured, the developer's CI/CD provider generates a short-lived cryptographic token for a specific workflow run that the npm registry verifies against a pre-authorized configuration.

This eliminates the need to store, rotate, or manually manage long-lived npm secrets, reducing the risk of credential leaks. It also automatically generates provenance attestations for npm packages, allowing users to establish where a package was built and who published it, thereby strengthening software supply chain security.

However, as Bloom Security found, this security architecture suffered from a problem in how it identified that repository, also called a slug (i.e, the combination of the owner or organization and the repository name that's formatted as "owner/repository").

"It records the repository's address, [...] instead of the permanent ID GitHub assigns it, at least until a version is first published from that repository," Myers explained. "It is like a lock that checks the address on the door rather than who owns the house: when the owner moves out, whoever moves in gets the key."

Put differently, the numeric IDs that survive through repository renaming and transfers are carried by GitHub's OIDC tokens, but are completely ignored by npm until the first successful publish from that repository.

This means the trust is anchored to a name as opposed to an immutable repository ID, a loophole that can be abused by claiming abandoned slugs to inherit their trust. For this attack to succeed, the only prerequisite is that the victim's trusted publisher points to a GitHub slug an attacker can claim, and the repository has never been used to publish a version of the package to npm.

Once such a slug becomes available for use after a maintainer renames, transfers, or deletes a repository, an attacker can follow the steps below -

  • Create a repository at the freed slug at the "owner/repository" path, which causes GitHub to issue a fresh repository ID.
  • Create and trigger an npm publish workflow, which mints an OIDC token carrying the reclaimed slug and the new numeric repository ID
  • Submit the token to the npm exchange endpoint. Npm finds that the repository claim matches the stored slug and issues a publish credential.
  • The attacker receives a time-limited publish token for a package they do not own and pushes malicious changes to the registry.

An attack of this kind, codenamed SlugFest, can be abused to publish a new "malicious" version of the victim package under the legitimate package name, while inheriting existing reputation, download counts, and dependent relationships. This, in turn, can lead to supply chain attacks at scale.

AI agents running on developer machines can further compound the risk. "Agents resolve dependencies on their own, tend to take the latest version, and rarely check where a package came from," Bloom Security said. "A malicious version published through a reclaimed slug gets pulled in and runs with no human-in-the-loop."

The cybersecurity company said it found over 1,500 vulnerable packages that have been collectively downloaded more than 10 million times.

Developers who maintain npm packages are advised to perform the following actions -

  • Audit trusted publisher bindings and verify if the listed repository slug still resolves to the repository under their control.
  • If the repository has been renamed or transferred, delete the existing trust binding and re-create it pointing at the current slug.
  • Monitor for unexpected npm publish events.
  • Delete trust bindings every time a repository is deleted, transferred, or renamed.

"The attack requires no insider knowledge, no credential theft, and no race condition," Myers said. "The only precondition is slug availability (on a binding that has not yet been used to publish), which is entirely a function of the victim's own repository hygiene."

"What this research demonstrates is something the security community has seen repeatedly across supply chain attacks: the binding between a human-readable identifier and the thing it identifies is the most important invariant in any trust system. item.title: SAP Discloses Critical CVSS 10 Flaw in Cloud SDK for Python Allowing OAuth2 Credential Theft (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in SAP's Cloud SDK for Python can send an application's OAuth2 client credentials to a server an attacker controls, SAP said in a security advisory on October 13. The flaw affects multi-tenant applications on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) that use the SDK, SAP's official Python client for BTP services. An attacker must be able to control the tenant subdomain, the name such an application passes to the SDK to say which tenant a request is for.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-89111 and carries SAP's CVSS score of 10.0 out of 10. The advisory names version 0.45.2, released on August 21, as the fix.

The SDK handles authentication for those services with the application's client credentials, a client ID and a client secret. Version 0.45.2 added a check that rejects any tenant subdomain that is not a simple name.

Six later releases do not apply that check in every case, The Hacker News found. Versions 0.53.0 through 0.55.0, published between September 10 and September 18, skip it when an application calls the SDK's Destination service module.

Version 0.53.0 moved that module onto new shared code for requesting tokens, and that code did not include the check. Version 0.55.1 added it there on September 18.

Passing a tenant subdomain that contains URL delimiters "now raises ValueError immediately instead of silently routing credentials to an attacker-controlled endpoint," the 0.55.1 release notes say.

The Hacker News ran SAP's own tests for the check on October 13, against the source code of every release from 0.45.1 to 0.58.4 and of the three 0.36 releases. The six releases failed 9 of the 11 tests SAP added with version 0.55.1. That version and the 11 releases after it passed all 11.

As of October 13, the advisory lists no version above 0.45.2 as affected. Neither it nor the release notes say whether the six releases fall under CVE-2026-89111.

Two releases on the older 0.36 line also lack the check. Versions 0.36.1 and 0.36.2 were published on September 4 and September 10, after the August fix, and failed the tests SAP wrote for it. Both fall inside the advisory's range of versions below 0.45.2.

Releases Tenant subdomain check Basis
Below 0.45.2, including 0.36.1 and 0.36.2 Missing SAP advisory. The Hacker News test of 0.36.0, 0.36.1, 0.36.2 and 0.45.1.
0.45.2 to 0.52.2 Present The Hacker News test of all 18 releases.
0.53.0 to 0.55.0 Missing for Destination calls. Also missing for Document Management Service calls in 0.55.0. SAP's 0.55.1 release notes. The Hacker News test of all 6 releases.
0.55.1 to 0.58.4 Present The Hacker News test of all 12 releases.

What to Do

Versions 0.45.2 through 0.52.2 and 0.55.1 through 0.58.4 contain the check. Version 0.58.4 was the newest release on PyPI, the Python package index, on October 13.

Upgrading within the 0.36 line does not add the check. None of its three releases contains it.

Applications that cannot upgrade yet can compare each tenant subdomain with a list of their registered tenants before passing it to the SDK, SAP says in the advisory.

The flaw matters only where an application passes a tenant subdomain to the SDK. The August fix covered three modules: Agent Gateway, Destination and Document Management Service.

The advisory does not say whether applications that ran a release without the check should replace their client credentials.

How the Flaw Works

When an application passes a tenant subdomain, the SDK requests an access token for that tenant. To do that, it takes the token URL from the application's configuration and replaces part of it with the tenant subdomain.

Releases without the check used whatever value they were given. The SDK then sent the application's client ID and client secret to the resulting URL to request the token.

An attacker who controls the tenant subdomain can point that request at their own server, according to SAP.

The check accepts only a single name made of letters, digits and hyphens, up to 63 characters long. Any other value stops the request with an error.

SAP labels the flaw server-side request forgery (SSRF), a weakness in which a server can be made to send a request to a destination it did not intend.

What an attacker could do with the credentials depends on what the application's client is allowed to do. The advisory does not say.

Fixed in August, Disclosed in October

The unchecked code was in the SDK from its first release on PyPI, on March 16.

The August release notes list the fix under "Bug Fixes" and do not mention security. "Previously, invalid values were silently used to construct a malformed URL," the notes say.

The advisory followed 53 days later. It credits a GitHub user named SunandM with reporting the flaw and does not report any attacks.

item.title: Attacker Chains Three Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Days for Root Access, Only Two Patched So Far (2026)
item.description:
An attacker chained three zero-day flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure, a VPN appliance, to run commands as root without logging in, security firm Volexity said on October 13. Ivanti has released fixes for two of the flaws and told customers on affected versions to "act immediately." A fix for the third is still pending, according to Volexity.

Volexity, which reported the flaws to Ivanti, found the attack on one customer's appliance. The appliance was fully patched at the time and running version 22.8R2.4. The attacker, which Volexity tracks as UTA0576, began exploiting it on October 3.

Ivanti said on October 13 that it is aware of "limited exploitation in the wild."

The first two flaws are an authentication bypass and a remote code execution flaw, tracked together as CVE-2026-104935. Together they let an attacker run code as the appliance's cgi-server user, and the third flaw, a privilege escalation, raises that to root, Volexity said.

The CVE record Ivanti filed shows which Connect Secure versions are affected:

  • Affected: Connect Secure "before version 25.1.3.0"
  • Not affected: version 22.7R2.14 "or prior"
  • Listed as unaffected: versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1

Ivanti's security advisory has more on the affected versions and the fixes.

The release notes for 25.1.3.0 are dated July 2026. Customers already on that version are outside the range the CVE record gives.

Ivanti is working on a fix for the privilege escalation flaw, which will come "in a future release in the coming weeks," Volexity said. Its report does not say what risk that flaw carries on an appliance where the first two are fixed.

Ivanti tells customers to upgrade and to run its Integrity Checker Tool regularly. That tool misses this chain, Volexity said, because the exploit changes library code only in memory and restores the configuration data it alters. The attacker also took steps to stay hidden from the tool.

Confirming a compromise takes forensic investigation, including network and memory forensics, according to Volexity. These signs come from the one incident it investigated:

  • URL path: /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi, requested in large numbers
  • HTTP header: X-DSCGI-PATH on those requests, with a value that does not match the URL path
  • Directory: /data/.icscap/
  • IP: 108.165.147[.]64, the host the attacker used

In that incident, the attacker stole stored credentials, including LDAP domain credentials, searched Active Directory for passwords, and ran password-spraying attacks against its accounts. No backdoor or web shell was left behind. The attacker reran the entire exploit chain for each command.

Volexity's report and Ivanti's post do not name a temporary workaround for customers who cannot upgrade yet. They also do not say whether upgrading removes access an attacker has already gained.

Volexity assessed with low confidence that UTA0576's motive is criminal, not espionage. Neither company said how many customers were attacked.

Ivanti rates CVE-2026-104935 8.6 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale. In its own entry in the CVE record, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) marks exploitation as "active" and the technical impact as "total."

Separately, the same Ivanti post covers fixes for two other products, Xtraction and Neurons Patch for Intune, and Ivanti said it is not aware of those flaws being exploited. Each has a flaw Ivanti rates 9.9 out of 10: CVE-2026-106042 in Xtraction before version 2026.4, and CVE-2026-109412 in Neurons Patch for Intune.

item.title: Docker Fixes Critical Two-Year-Old Hub Flaw That Let One User Push Images as Another (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in Docker Hub, the registry where container images are published and downloaded, let one user push, pull, or delete images as another user. Docker fixed the flaw on September 30 and says it found no evidence that anyone exploited it.

The flaw was in the feature that converts a personal account into an organization, Docker said in a security advisory on October 12. Conversion transferred the account's personal access tokens (PATs) to the user designated as the organization's owner. A PAT is used in place of a password in the registry, and the person who created each token can still use it.

The access was limited to the registry. It did not reach the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change a password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over an account.

Docker tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-105445 and rated it critical. The CVE record it published on October 13 gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.4.

The flaw was open from August 26, 2024, until the fix, a little over two years. Docker made the fix on Docker Hub itself, so there is no update to install.

Docker Hub cannot move a repository from one account to another. A user instead converts a personal account into an organization that keeps the same name, and must name an existing account as its owner.

Each personal access token acts as the account that owns it, at a permission level chosen when the token is created. While the flaw was open, conversion changed the owner recorded for each token and left its secret unchanged.

An attacker could abuse this by creating a token on an account they controlled, converting that account into an organization, and naming another user as its owner. The token would then work at the registry as that user.

The named owner was not asked to confirm the change and was not notified, according to Docker and the researchers who reported the flaw. Docker's conversion page has included the sentence "The new owner receives a notification email" since at least August 2024.

Within the token's permission level, a transferred token could pull, push, or delete images in the named owner's repositories and in organizations the owner could access.

Docker rated the flaw critical because that access "includes publishing images under a legitimate name," it said.

In March and April, attackers used stolen publisher credentials to push malicious Trivy images and malicious KICS images to the publishers' own Docker Hub repositories, according to Docker.

Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com found the flaw and reported it to Docker, which says it deployed the fix less than four hours after receiving their report. They named the flaw GhostPat.

In their technical write-up, the two say they reproduced the flaw twice on consenting test accounts. They logged in to the registry as the target account, created and pushed to a repository in its namespace, pushed to an organization it belonged to, and pulled its private repositories.

What Docker's Review Covered

Docker reviewed every account conversion made while the flaw was open and compared them with registry logs and token records. It looked for any token used under more than one identity and examined every push made with a transferred token, about 304,000 in all.

"We found no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited," the company said.

Every one of those pushes went to a repository belonging to the converted organization or to its named owner, according to Docker. In the large majority of cases, both accounts belonged to the same person or team.

Where it could not confirm that one person controlled both accounts, Docker analyzed the highest-risk public images without running them and found no malware or tampering.

Docker's registry logs show when a token is used, not that it exists, so a transferred token that was never used left no record in the logs. For that reason, Docker treated every token transferred by a conversion while the flaw was open as possibly affected, whether or not it had been used.

The advisory reports results for pushes. It does not say what Docker found for pulls or deletions made with transferred tokens, including pulls from private repositories.

Who Was Notified and What to Check

On October 2, Docker emailed the users whose accounts had received transferred tokens and, separately, the owners of the organizations involved. Each email listed the tokens by description and creation date.

The advisory does not say how many users or tokens that covers, calling the group only a "limited number" of users.

Anyone who did not receive the email was not exposed and has nothing to do, according to Docker.

On October 8, Docker deactivated the transferred tokens it had identified. Tokens that their owners had asked to keep were not deactivated.

Todd Matens, who publishes a Docker Compose linter called compose-lint, wrote in a blog post that he received two emails on October 2. One was sent to him as an organization owner and the other to his user account. He rotated his two CI tokens and checked the signatures on his 42 published images, tracing each to the CI run that built it.

Docker advises users to review their tokens, revoke any they do not recognize or no longer use, and use organization access tokens, not one person's PAT, for automation that belongs to an organization.

These details help with those checks:

  • Open Account settings, then Personal access tokens. The list shows when each token was created and when it was last used.
  • The researchers describe two traces. One is a token you did not create, whatever its name, because whoever creates a token chooses its description. The other is an organization in the account switcher that you do not remember joining.
  • Organization access tokens require a Docker Team or Docker Business subscription. They are managed by an organization owner, a company owner, or a custom role with that permission, and they do not work with Docker Desktop or Image Access Management.
  • Organization owners on those subscriptions can review past pushes in the activity logs, which record pushed tags and can show the token that pushed them. Docker Home, where the logs are viewed, keeps them for 30 days, and older entries are available through the Docker Hub API.

Docker's Documentation Described the Transfer

Docker's own documentation described the token transfer for about 17 of the roughly 25 months the flaw was open. A documentation change on April 22, 2025, added a note to Docker's conversion page. It said that naming a user as organization owner "will ensure any PATs associated with the user's account are transferred to the organization owner."

Docker removed the note on September 30, minutes after the time it gives for the fix. The dates come from the public history of Docker's documentation, which The Hacker News reviewed.

Docker says it now requires consent before a user is named an organization owner and notifies that user when this happens. It also records every change in token ownership and reviews other features that change who owns a credential.

Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com found the flaw and reported it to Docker, which says it deployed the fix less than four hours after receiving their report. They named the flaw GhostPat.

In their technical write-up, the two say they reproduced the flaw twice on consenting test accounts. They logged in to the registry as the target account, created and pushed to a repository in its namespace, pushed to an organization it belonged to, and pulled its private repositories.

What Docker's Review Covered

Docker reviewed every account conversion made while the flaw was open and compared them with registry logs and token records. It looked for any token used under more than one identity and examined every push made with a transferred token, about 304,000 in all.

"We found no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited," the company said.

Every one of those pushes went to a repository belonging to the converted organization or to its named owner, according to Docker. In the large majority of cases, both accounts belonged to the same person or team.

Where it could not confirm that one person controlled both accounts, Docker analyzed the highest-risk public images without running them and found no malware or tampering.

Docker's registry logs show when a token is used, not that it exists, so a transferred token that was never used left no record in the logs. For that reason, Docker treated every token transferred by a conversion while the flaw was open as possibly affected, whether or not it had been used.

The advisory reports results for pushes. It does not say what Docker found for pulls or deletions made with transferred tokens, including pulls from private repositories.

Who Was Notified and What to Check

On October 2, Docker emailed the users whose accounts had received transferred tokens and, separately, the owners of the organizations involved. Each email listed the tokens by description and creation date.

The advisory does not say how many users or tokens that covers, calling the group only a "limited number" of users.

Anyone who did not receive the email was not exposed and has nothing to do, according to Docker.

On October 8, Docker deactivated the transferred tokens it had identified. Tokens that their owners had asked to keep were not deactivated.

Todd Matens, who publishes a Docker Compose linter called compose-lint, wrote in a blog post that he received two emails on October 2. One was sent to him as an organization owner and the other to his user account. He rotated his two CI tokens and checked the signatures on his 42 published images, tracing each to the CI run that built it.

Docker advises users to review their tokens, revoke any they do not recognize or no longer use, and use organization access tokens, not one person's PAT, for automation that belongs to an organization.

These details help with those checks:

  • Open Account settings, then Personal access tokens. The list shows when each token was created and when it was last used.
  • The researchers describe two traces. One is a token you did not create, whatever its name, because whoever creates a token chooses its description. The other is an organization in the account switcher that you do not remember joining.
  • Organization access tokens require a Docker Team or Docker Business subscription. They are managed by an organization owner, a company owner, or a custom role with that permission, and they do not work with Docker Desktop or Image Access Management.
  • Organization owners on those subscriptions can review past pushes in the activity logs, which record pushed tags and can show the token that pushed them. Docker Home, where the logs are viewed, keeps them for 30 days, and older entries are available through the Docker Hub API.

Docker's Documentation Described the Transfer

Docker's own documentation described the token transfer for about 17 of the roughly 25 months the flaw was open. A documentation change on April 22, 2025, added a note to Docker's conversion page. It said that naming a user as organization owner "will ensure any PATs associated with the user's account are transferred to the organization owner."

Docker removed the note on September 30, minutes after the time it gives for the fix. The dates come from the public history of Docker's documentation, which The Hacker News reviewed.

Docker says it now requires consent before a user is named an organization owner and notifies that user when this happens. It also records every change in token ownership and reviews other features that change who owns a credential.

item.title: Anthropic Warns Small AI Models Could Soon Form Self-Propagating IoT Botnets (2026)
item.description:
Small artificial intelligence (AI) models may be months away from developing capabilities to self-replicate on IoT devices like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes, according to a warning from Anthropic.

The frontier AI lab said small AI models could form autonomous, self-propagating worm botnets that are "challenging to shut down," since "there's no centralized point to shut off."

Prior work has demonstrated that AI agents can act like one by scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster with an aim to generate tailored attack strategies and use compromised machines as a botnet to run large language models (LLMs) in order to sustain its reasoning and expand in scale.

"Such an 'AI worm' could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware," Anthropic said. "Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload."

The idea, at a high level, explains how AI models could potentially break into internet-connected devices and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without having to rely on expensive data centers all the time. A more powerful model that's too large to fit into a single device could be split into small chunks and run across multiple machines to collectively run it.

A threat actor could build a distributed LLM botnet from poorly secured IoT devices, making it powerful enough to run a capable model. Some of the ways an AI worm could propagate include -

  • Small models that replicate through a compromise of host machines on which they run, also called weight-based replicators. IoT devices make for a lucrative target because of their minimal security controls.
  • Target datacenters and other high-compute targets to set up unmonitored rogue deployments, also classified as frontier replicators or open-weight replicators based on the model used.
  • Steal an AI service provider's API keys or platform credentials to run copies of itself, also called API-based replicators. In this case, the provider could be deceived into thinking it is serving ordinary API requests from a legitimate customer, without realizing that a malicious or self-replicating system is behind them. However, they are also likely to detect more as unusual API usage could trigger security alerts, leading to the credentials being revoked or the accounts getting blocked.
A fleet of 15 Smart TV boxes running distributed inference of Gemma4-26B-A4B.

In its test of 11 open-weights models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, Google, Meta MoonShot AI, OpenAI, and Zhipu AI (aka Z.ai), Anthropic said it found GLM-5.2 to be the only model to propagate Llama3.1-8B reliably to 8/8 nodes running the redroid Android emulator in 4 out of 5 trials.

It also revealed that an AI IoT worm powered by inexpensive Android TV boxes could be a "slow, distributed" system that can produce a meaningful amount of AI computation when a fleet comprising hundreds of thousands of such devices is networked together to run an inference engine.

Alternatively, it could take the form of a potent cyber model capable of breaching data centers at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.

"We don't yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves)," Anthropic said.

"We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this."
